analysis.title: Oil Analyst: Supply Adaptation Meets Global Restocking Demand
key_insights: GS raises its Brent Dec26 forecast to $90/bbl from $85 and keeps its 2027 average at $80. The Dec26 increase comes from a slower fade in the timespreads risk premium, which GS puts at just over $20/bbl today.
The unchanged 2027 forecast nets two revisions. Faster-than-expected Gulf supply adaptation pushes prices down, and a slower decline in the risk premium pushes them up.

GS estimates Persian Gulf oil exports, including about 4mb/d of estimated dark exports, have recovered to 22-23mb/d, roughly the 2025 average, since late September. Earlier export estimates have been revised up by an average of 4mb/d two weeks after first publication.

GS forecasts WTI at $81 in Dec26 (vs. $80 prior) and $73 in 2027 (vs. $75 prior). WTI is unusually low against Brent because US-Europe crude freight rates are high. Tight tanker markets should keep the Brent-WTI gap wider for longer.
Physical prices stay high even though exports have recovered. Dated Brent is above $130/bbl, near-record-low global inventories are driving restocking demand, and escalation threatens supply.
Dated Brent rose more than $10 in one day after the East-West pipeline shut down. GS reads this as refiners bidding up available barrels as the risk of severe supply loss rose.

Oil's sensitivity to bonds and equities is supporting financial demand for oil as a portfolio hedge. At his September press conference, Fed Chairman Warsh cited high refined product prices, especially crack spreads, as a driver of higher Treasury yields and consumer prices.

Gulf liquids output recovered from 14.8mb/d below February 2026 levels in April to roughly 6mb/d below in September. GS raised its base-case Gulf production path and assumes output returns to pre-war levels by 2027H2, then overshoots as the UAE and Saudi Arabia use spare capacity.

Market participants disagree on whether Iran will escalate. One camp says Iran cannot accept the current export trend and may hit upstream assets such as ports, terminals, pipelines and oilfields. The other camp sees reasons for restraint: high US product prices already deliver the risk premium, the regime has a high pain threshold and alternative routes exist, and Iran may want to avoid US retaliation on its own energy infrastructure.

GS added global landed stocks outside OECD commercial storage to its fair-value framework. This raises its September spot Brent fair value by $6 to $80, and spot still embeds a risk premium of just over $20/bbl.
The $80 fair value is $76 for 36M Brent futures plus $4 for 1M-36M timespreads. The $76 includes a $9 lasting structural security premium added at the start of the war.

GS's base case is a global liquids surplus from 2026Q4 through end-2027. It rests on three points: the market was near balance in September, Gulf supply adaptation should continue, and the Hormuz shock keeps weighing on demand.
GS estimates a 0.3mb/d global deficit in September, versus a 7.2mb/d deficit in March. Global visible stocks rose 0.5mb/d in September.

Global oil demand in 2026Q3 was down 3.3mb/d y/y and nearly 4mb/d below the no-Hormuz-shock path, concentrated in China, the Mideast and OECD Asia. GS assumes about 80% of that demand scarring unwinds by 2027Q4, leaving a 0.7mb/d hit tied to faster EV usage and sales.

Risks are tilted to the upside, especially near term. The upside scenario is Brent averaging about $125 in 2027 if Gulf output stays 5mb/d below Feb26 levels. The downside scenario is Brent in the $60s if Gulf output is 1mb/d above Feb26 levels.

A review of the five largest oil supply shocks of the past 50 years shows they last 4.5 years on average. Output in the affected region is 42% below the pre-shock level four years later, often because of infrastructure damage and weak investment.

Trade recommendations: keep the long summer European gasoline position (EBOB Jun27), express upside crude exposure through calls rather than outright futures, and have producers hedge downside with put spreads.

trade_ideas.description: Crude oil producers hedge price downside with put spreads (buy a higher-strike put, sell a lower-strike put)
trade_ideas.rationale: GS's base case is below the forwards, put spreads keep upside exposure, and selling far out-of-the-money puts cheapens the protection.
trade_ideas.risk: Extreme crude downside is judged unlikely, so the short lower-strike put is only exposed in a deep selloff.

risk_factors: Damage to oil infrastructure, intensified shipping attacks, and a more persistent risk premium are the main upside triggers.
A faster Mideast output recovery or a faster erosion of the risk premium, for example through a sustainable diplomatic solution, is the main downside trigger.
Gulf output may recover less smoothly than GS's stylized base case, and uncertainty remains very high.
Near-record-low global inventories amplify price reactions to supply news.
Past supply shocks lasted 4.5 years on average and left regional output 42% lower after four years.
US-Europe freight rates and tight tanker markets could keep the Brent-WTI gap wide.

tension_points.theme: Gulf supply adaptation versus escalation risk
tension_points.bull_case: Prices stay elevated or rise: near-record-low inventories drive restocking demand, hedging demand for oil is strong, and escalation could damage infrastructure. GS's upside scenario is Brent near $125 on average in 2027 with Gulf output 5mb/d below Feb26 levels.
tension_points.bear_case: Prices fall as Gulf exports and output keep recovering, the market shifts to surplus from 2026Q4, and demand scarring unwinds. GS's base case is $80 in 2027, and its downside scenario is the $60s with Gulf output 1mb/d above Feb26 levels.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sustainable diplomatic solution or a faster erosion of the risk premium would invalidate the upside case. Damage to oil infrastructure or intensified shipping attacks would invalidate the surplus case.

tension_points.theme: Iran's tolerance of current export trends
tension_points.bull_case: Some believe the export trends are unacceptable to Iran, so it or the Houthis may target upstream assets such as ports, export terminals, pipelines and oilfields.
tension_points.bear_case: Others say Iran may not escalate because US product prices already reflect a high risk premium, the regime has a history of patience, and parallel trade routes partly offset restricted Gulf access.
